Fast money is leaving, patient money is arriving—and RBI quietly rewrites the rules

Although RBI's measures were not explicitly termed capital controls, they function as such and their effectiveness will influence the rupee’s trajectory in the coming months.

Bidisha Bhattacharya

27 October, 2026 08:00 am IST

Text Size: A- A+

-->

I n early October, several stakeholders, including families with children studying abroad, importers awaiting shipments, and motorists monitoring fuel prices, experienced heightened anxiety. On Friday, 9 October, the Indian rupee closed the week at about Rs 96.7 to the dollar, near the record low seen in May. At the same time, India’s foreign exchange reserves had declined for five consecutive weeks, foreign investors had consistently divested from Indian equities, and oil prices had exceeded $100 per barrel. Subsequently, the Reserve Bank of India quietly implemented strategic changes, and, within a week, the rupee appreciated to nearly Rs 95.

The RBI’s intervention targeted rapid capital movement. It reduced the permissible size of currency derivative transactions lacking an underlying trade from $100 million to $5 million, prohibited companies from cancelling and rebooking hedges for speculative purposes, mandated banks to maintain a 20 per cent cash reserve with the RBI against large forward dollar purchase contracts, and established a special facility to sell dollars directly to state-run oil companies, thereby excluding their transactions from the open market. Although these measures were not explicitly termed capital controls, they effectively function as such, and their effectiveness will influence the rupee’s trajectory in the coming months.

Six weeks that emptied the cushion To understand the rationale behind the RBI’s actions, it helps to examine developments during the summer. Between mid-July and early September, foreign exchange reserves increased by approximately $110 billion over seven weeks, reaching a record high of $785.7 billion on 4 September. This significant increase reflected a major capital influx, including special dollar deposits from Indians abroad, which, as I noted in my September column , attracted far more funds than anticipated.

Show Full Article

Note: Rupee rate is implied by dividing the rupee value of total reserves by their dollar value in each week’s table. Dashed line marks the RBI’s foreign exchange measures announced on 10 October 2026. Over the next six weeks, the financial cushion shrank as reserves fell by $64.7 billion, or 8.2 per cent, to $721 billion by 16 October. This decline occurred as the RBI intervened by selling dollars to stabilise the rupee amid an escalating oil bill driven by the Gulf crisis. By mid-October, foreign exchange reserves had returned to levels similar to those observed in mid-August.

In the early 1960s, Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming demonstrated that a nation cannot simultaneously maintain a stable currency, free capital movement, and an independent interest rate policy. This principle, known as the “impossible trinity,” necessitates the relinquishment of one of these three objectives. The RBI aimed to stabilise the rupee while independently setting interest rates for India, rather than aligning with Washington’s policies. Consequently, on 10 October, it imposed restrictions on capital flows.

Also read: Rupee’s story is not just its exchange rate with the US. It’s about REER—a corrective lens

Not all foreign money is the same Proponents argue that such restrictions deter investors; however, foreign capital takes two distinct forms.

Between April and August, portfolio investors who trade listed shares withdrew about $9.9 billion from Indian equities. An additional $8.8 billion was withdrawn in September and October. In contrast, during the same April-August period, net foreign direct investment inflows, characterised as patient capital that builds factories and takes long-term stakes in companies, rose to $13.8 billion, up from $9.6 billion the previous year.

Hélène Rey of the London Business School explained this divergence in a notable 2013 lecture at Jackson Hole. She argued that portfolio capital operates within a “global financial cycle” influenced by US interest rates and global economic apprehensions, regardless of a country’s economic performance, including India’s. Her analysis concluded that the trilemma is essentially a dilemma: a nation seeking to maintain control over its interest rates must regulate volatile capital flows. This approach aligns with the Reserve Bank of India’s strategy, which targets speculative activities while preserving long-term investments. Even the International Monetary Fund, historically an advocate for unrestricted capital flows, acknowledged in 2012 that temporary measures of this nature can be prudent during economic turbulence.

The 2013 playbook, played from strength India has faced a similar situation before. In May 2013, the United States Federal Reserve indicated a potential reduction in its market support, leading to a significant withdrawal of capital from emerging economies, an event referred to as the “taper tantrum.”

In 2013, the Indian rupee depreciated from about Rs 55 to over Rs 66 against the dollar within fifteen weeks, a loss of nearly 20 per cent, while foreign reserves fell by only about 6 per cent. The RBI implemented a series of measures, including restrictions on overseas investments in August, the establishment of a dollar window for oil companies on 28 August, and the introduction of a scheme on Raghuram Rajan’s first day as Governor that attracted substantial dollar deposits from Indians abroad. These interventions helped the rupee recover, leading to the subsequent withdrawal of the measures.

In contrast, the current scenario has seen the RBI expend a larger proportion of its reserves, approximately 8 per cent, while the rupee has depreciated by less than 2.5 per cent at its weakest point. This strategic choice is feasible for a nation with reserves about 2.5 times higher than in 2013, though it is not sustainable indefinitely. The current objective is to ensure the effectiveness of these measures and subsequently withdraw them. Markets are more amenable to temporary restrictions on rapid capital flows when there is a clear exit strategy.

Therefore, announcing a review date or linking the regulations to specific indicators, such as oil prices or reserve levels, would reassure investors that these measures are temporary. Additionally, the government should actively engage with long-term investors, as Indian companies invested $17.7 billion abroad in the first five months of the current fiscal year, offsetting the benefits of foreign investment inflows. Ultimately, the most robust defence is domestic: increased investment by Indian households and institutions in local markets would mitigate the impact of foreign capital withdrawal on the rupee.

The situation remains precarious. Should oil prices rise further or foreign capital outflows resume, the RBI will face renewed challenges. Unlike in 2013, when India could only watch the rupee decline and respond reactively, in 2026 the country has been able to intervene, at least temporarily. The sustainability of this intervention depends on factors beyond the RBI’s control, such as oil prices, US Federal Reserve policy, and how quickly the current restrictions can be lifted.

Bidisha Bhattacharya is ThePrint Consulting Editor (Economics) and an Associate Fellow, Chintan Research Foundation. She tweets @Bidishabh. Views are personal.

By Maayan Lubell JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) – Israel holds a parliamentary election on Tuesday, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.

WHEN WILL WE KNOW WHO WON?

Show Full Article

It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.

Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and ends at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT), when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.

A clear picture may emerge quickly but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.

The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.

WHY IS IT SO COMPLICATED?

Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be held every four years but early elections have been frequent.

The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.

About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE RESULTS ARE PUBLISHED?

After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.

That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.

No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.

If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.

(Reporting by Maayan Lubell, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

Serbia’s new leaders face host of tough challenges

Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

(Corrects paragraph 15 to say top student leaders had not said whether a future government would halt weapons exports)

BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) – Serbia’s student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday’s parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.

Here are a few of them:

Show Full Article

KOSOVO

The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students’ candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue.

Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo’s Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency.

FRAYED EU RELATIONS

With Serbia’s European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues.

Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc.

The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires  Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc stood ready to support reforms including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU.

COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM

The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the sale of Russia’s stake in energy company NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL.

Russia’s Gazprom is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency.

The Student List’s top candidates had not said whether a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

CORRUPTION

The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests.

They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget.

Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students’ anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds.

Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.

ECONOMY

Serbia’s economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows.

The IMF has forecast Serbia’s economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August’s 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024.

The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights.

Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups.

The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work.

Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication.

(Reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)
